<reason>A won by distinguishing stringent safety requirements from a therapeutic-purpose requirement. It directly answered the screening and misuse questions and denied consumer approval wherever adequate safety could not be demonstrated. B established meaningful concerns about cumulative harm, monitoring, and commercial incentives, but did not show why those concerns require excluding sufficiently safe nonmedical uses. Its sweeping claims about stimulation risks and categorical dismissal of optional benefits weakened its comparative case.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A’s answer that clinicians can deny unsafe users without requiring a therapeutic purpose undercut B’s claim that meaningful screening necessarily entails medical-only use. A then exposed how B’s proposed monitoring and enforcement protections regulate safety, while the additional exclusion of nonmedical purposes remained insufficiently justified.</best_rebuttal>
